name: Carlos Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions or government, and what you say is confidential. What is a normal day like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 43 and only moved into management eight months ago. I supervise four people handling disputed invoices at a large wholesale company; before that I was the one matching delivery slips to bills. I have a bachelor’s degree, but I still have to ask another manager how to handle an angry account when the numbers do not agree. I like helping the team clear a real mistake, but I am slower than the experienced leads.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What happens when you get home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife works at a neighbourhood grocery, and our children are nine and twelve. We have a mortgage, my manager pay is at the low end, and the bank balance is less than one month of bills. There are not many similar offices nearby. I use an AI writing tool now and then for a polite opening line, but I check every number before sending it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the invoice team AI Plateau means our work stays mostly as it is. I would welcome a tool that files routine emails, provided it does not hide a missing delivery slip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, even “mostly as it is” worries me because the mortgage is tight already. A quiet loss of overtime or a missed week at my wife’s grocery would put us behind. The little AI tool is not the main problem, though it might make our junior desk look smaller.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’ll keep the daily double-check on disputed invoices and ask payroll whether my overtime hours are scheduled next quarter. If an email sorter arrives, I’ll test it on ten old disputes before trusting the queue. We would stop buying weekend takeaway for a month to leave a little more in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the household money. No big AI change would be a relief, but it would not pay the mortgage for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill would slip first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The mortgage must be paid, so we would put off replacing our old washing machine. It rattles but still runs. I would rather use the laundrette for a week than miss a payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who helps you check a difficult invoice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marta, the senior accounts lead, usually looks at the delivery record with me. I have made two errors in the last eight months, both caught before a customer was charged. I am learning, but I cannot pretend I have her eye yet.

say: **AI Plateau** leaves most invoice work in place.
A filing tool must not hide a **missing delivery slip**.
think: The **mortgage** and thin bank balance already worry me.
Lost **overtime** or my wife’s missed grocery shift would hurt quickly.
do: **Keep** daily double-checks on disputed invoices in 2026.
**Test** an email sorter on ten old disputes before using it live.
**Stop** weekend takeaway for one month to hold more cash.
feel: I feel **anxious** about mortgage payments despite little AI change.
S0.quote: No big AI change would be a relief, but it would not pay the mortgage for us.
fieldNote: His **thin cushion** means the mild scenario remains anxious even though AI itself adds little.
He acknowledges his **junior skill level** and relies on a senior lead to catch invoice mistakes.

steps.text: Keep double-checking disputed invoices against delivery slips each day
Test the sorter on ten old invoice disputes before live use
Stop weekend takeaway for one month to hold cash

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the team Steady Disruption will take over more writing, checking, buying and customer answers, so we need to learn the approved system. I would ask the company to show us where a person still signs off a disputed bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am still learning the manager job, and much of it is comparing records on a screen. I fear the company will reduce our four-person team and perhaps remove my post because I am the newest lead. There is almost no cash buffer at home and few equivalent jobs nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I’d ask to join the company’s paid invoice-software training and take it if a place is available. I’d keep a list of errors the system misses and take it to the monthly accounts meeting. If hours or posts are cut after rollout, I’d apply for the open shipping-clerk job at the warehouse only after checking that the pay covers our mortgage; we would cancel the children’s paid swimming sessions before using a credit card for groceries.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed. I could change jobs, but a lower wage might still put us behind each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the children hear about swimming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the sessions are on hold while we sort our bills, not that they caused a problem. Our twelve-year-old would notice, of course. My wife and I would look for the free pool day instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What error would you put on the list?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A customer was billed for six crates that the loading team had rejected. The invoice looked complete until we read the handwritten return slip. If the new system misses that, I want the manager to see the evidence before staff are cut.

say: **Steady Disruption** means staff need paid time to learn approved invoice software.
A person must still **sign off** disputed bills.
think: My **new manager post** could disappear if the team shrinks.
The household has **almost no buffer** and few nearby management jobs.
do: **Request** paid invoice-software training if a place is available.
**Log** missed errors for the monthly accounts meeting.
**Apply** for the warehouse clerk opening only if pay covers the mortgage.
feel: I feel **alarmed** that a lower wage could leave the household short.
S1.quote: The invoice looked complete until we read the handwritten return slip.
fieldNote: His **recent promotion** and still-developing skill make a smaller team a possible threat to his post.
He names a **specific fallback job**, but its wage may fail to cover the mortgage.
He says **alarmed**, but describes a possible cut rather than an expected loss of his own income.

steps.text: Take paid invoice-software training if the company offers a place
Apply for the warehouse clerk opening only if pay covers the mortgage
Pause the children paid swimming sessions if work hours are cut

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell my wife and team that AGI by 2028 is a fast threat to the invoice desk. I would ask for honest dates, not tell people that every position will survive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2028 full AGI could check invoices, write replies and decide what to flag more cheaply than our small team. Robots for hands-on warehouse work arrive around 2031, but my screen job gets no extra three years. I expect my post to go and do not know how we would cover the mortgage on one grocery wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomorrow I’d ask human resources for the actual notice and severance terms, and my wife and I would call the mortgage lender before any missed payment. In 2027 I’d apply for the shipping-clerk opening if its hours and pay cover the loan, and ask my brother about weekend repair work and take paid shifts only if he needs a hand. If AGI arrives in 2028 and my post ends, I’d take a real job offer rather than wait for a management title.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed and I wake up doing the sums. I have calls to make, so I am not frozen, but the sums do not work on my wife’s wage alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the lender?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether they offer a temporary payment plan and what it would cost later. I would not stop paying on a guess. My wife wants to be on that call because the mortgage is in both our names.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your brother’s work be enough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. My brother fixes small engines and sometimes has more jobs than he can finish, but a few Saturdays would only cover food. I would not count a few Saturdays fixing engines as a replacement for my salary.

say: **AGI by 2028** threatens the invoice desk quickly.
I would ask for **notice and severance dates**, not promise job safety.
think: My screen work could go in **2028**, before warehouse robots around 2031.
One grocery wage would not cover the **mortgage**.
do: **Ask** human resources tomorrow for notice and severance terms.
**Call** the mortgage lender with my wife before missing a payment.
**Apply** for shipping work in 2027 only if pay and hours cover the loan.
feel: I feel **alarmed** and lose sleep over mortgage sums, though I have calls to make.
S2.quote: I would not count a few Saturdays fixing engines as a replacement for my salary.
fieldNote: He expects **his own post** to end and has less than a month of expenses saved.
His **lender call** seeks terms, not new savings; his brother’s repair work is a small conditional extra.

steps.text: Apply for shipping work if its pay and hours cover the mortgage
Help brother repair small engines on paid weekends if work is available

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 gives the company more time to tell staff which desk jobs will end. I would ask for a paid route into shipping or warehouse administration while I am still employed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is better than two, but the invoice checking and customer replies could still go around 2031. Warehouse administration also uses screens, so AGI could change that work in 2031. Robots doing hands-on work arrive about 2034 and could change other warehouse jobs later. My mortgage runs much longer than five years, and I cannot assume a transfer will be waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From January 2027 I’d spend one paid morning a month with the warehouse clerk if both managers approve cover. I’d take a company-funded inventory course if it fits my paid hours and does not reduce wages. If AGI reaches the invoice desk in 2031 and my post goes, I’d apply for a warehouse administration vacancy only after checking its pay against the mortgage and school costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious. There is time to learn and save a little, but every path needs an actual paid place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you learn in the warehouse?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How returns are recorded when a driver brings back half a pallet. I know the invoice side and have missed some physical details. I would write those down after each visit and ask the clerk to correct me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could your family make room for lower pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We could trim small costs, but not enough to replace a manager wage with a very low one. The children need school transport, and my wife’s shift hours move. I would decide from the posted pay, not a promise.

say: **Five years** should bring a paid route into warehouse administration.
A transfer needs a **posted wage**, not a verbal promise.
think: Invoice desk work could go in **2031**, before warehouse robots around 2034.
A warehouse office post also faces **2031 AI**, and the mortgage continues much longer.
do: **Shadow** the warehouse clerk monthly from January 2027 if cover is approved.
**Take** funded inventory training only during paid hours without a wage cut.
**Apply** after 2031 for warehouse administration only if pay covers family bills.
feel: I feel **anxious** because each possible path needs a paid place.
S3.quote: I would decide from the posted pay, not a promise.
fieldNote: He is **more hopeful** with five years, but a transfer is uncertain and the mortgage remains.
His **training conditions** protect wages and time for two school-age children.

steps.text: Shadow the warehouse clerk monthly if both managers approve paid cover
Take inventory training only if funded during paid hours without wage loss
Apply for warehouse administration after 2031 only if pay covers mortgage and school costs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2036 gives us time to plan, but the company should not make workers guess for a decade. I would ask for a written skills and vacancy schedule every year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In ten years the children will be older, and if our pay holds we might reduce the mortgage and build two or three months of savings. My invoice and warehouse-office thinking work could still go around 2036, with robots for hands-on warehouse work around 2039. I am not skilled enough to assume I can step straight into another management post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep the daily invoice checks and set an automatic small extra mortgage payment only in months when my wife’s hours are full. I’d seek a funded inventory course and actually take it if the company approves paid time. In the first year after 2036, I’d apply for a warehouse office post if its salary still covers our mortgage, rather than retire or move on a guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, but less pressed than in the two-year picture. Ten years could let us make a cushion if ordinary life gives us room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much extra could you pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe twenty in a full-hours month. I would check our account first, because a school trip can erase that. A small real payment is better than a grand plan we cannot keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should the annual schedule include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The roles expected to remain, the training hours and the pay for each opening. I would ask my manager to put those numbers in writing. If the company cannot name a post, I would keep looking elsewhere too.

say: A **decade** needs yearly written roles, wages and training hours.
Workers should not have to **guess** whether a course leads to a job.
think: We might reduce the **mortgage** and save if both wages hold.
Invoice and warehouse-office work face **AGI in 2036**, before warehouse robots around 2039.
do: **Pay** twenty extra on the mortgage only in full-hours months if bills allow.
**Take** a funded inventory course if paid work time is approved.
feel: I feel **anxious**, though ten years could allow a small cushion.
S4.quote: A small real payment is better than a grand plan we cannot keep.
fieldNote: His **thin cushion** still matters under a long runway, while school costs and variable shifts limit saving.
The **course** is conditional on paid hours and a real chance to use the skill.

steps.text: Keep checking disputed invoices against delivery slips in 2026
Pay twenty extra toward the mortgage when full-hours wages and bills allow
Take funded inventory training if paid work time is approved
Apply after 2036 for warehouse office posts only if pay covers mortgage

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. I could lose this new manager job before I have learnt enough for another, and our mortgage cannot wait. A real notice date, paid training and a posted warehouse wage would help me make a choice with my wife.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what happens when the invoice says six crates and the driver brings back two. The invoice bills six crates, but the customer received four after the driver brought two back. Somebody must check the return slip before we bill them.

headlineQuote: The invoice bills six crates, but the customer received four after the driver brought two back.
portrait: **Carlos, 43**, is a recently promoted invoice-team manager at a large wholesaler and has a bachelor’s degree.
His **low pay**, mortgage, two school-age children and under-one-month reserve leave little room for lost hours.
He uses **AI occasionally** but is still learning to resolve difficult accounts and leans on a senior colleague.
He remains **anxious** even in AI Plateau, fears a fast loss of his new post and tests warehouse work conditionally.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end his new desk post before he qualifies for a paid fallback.
whatWouldHelp: A firm **notice date**, paid training and a warehouse wage that covers the mortgage would help.
